arXiv:2603.29127v5 [math.CO] 28 Aug 2026

C4C_{4}-Free Subgraphs of the Hypercubes Q6Q_{6}, Q7Q_{7}, and Q8Q_{8}:
Odd Squares, Fully Frustrated Models, and Computational Structure

Minamo Minamoto Affiliation: Independent Email: minamominamoto4f5683f6@gmail.com
March 2026 (revised August 2026)
Abstract

We study C4C_{4}-free subgraphs of the hypercubes Q6Q_{6}, Q7Q_{7} and Q8Q_{8}. Writing g⁡(n)g(n) for the maximum size of an odd-square edge set — one meeting every 44-cycle (square) of QnQ_{n} in exactly one or three edges — we prove g⁡(6)=132g(6)=132, g⁡(7)=304g(7)=304 and g⁡(8)=682g(8)=682, give matching explicit machine-verifiable edge-list certificates, and hence obtain ex⁡(Q7,C4)≥304\mathrm{ex}(Q_{7},C_{4})\geq 304 and ex⁡(Q8,C4)≥682\mathrm{ex}(Q_{8},C_{4})\geq 682. Under the standard correspondence with fully frustrated signed hypercubes these values are already implicit in the statistical-physics literature: the field identity, the integer optimisation it feeds, and its optimal values go back to Derrida, Pomeau, Toulouse and Vannimenus (DPTV, 1979), who also construct ground states for D≤7D\leq 7; the D=8D=8 attainment was reported, without any released configuration, by Marinari, Parisi and Ritort (MPR, 1995); and Laplante, Naserasr, Sunny and Wang treat the graph-theoretic formulation directly. Our contribution is accordingly narrow and explicit: a short self-contained proof of the optima via a mod-88 refinement of the classical two-point inequality; the certificates themselves, with dependency-free verifiers; and an exhaustive decision of the realisability of the optimal n=6n=6 field distributions — settling in proof form the question DPTV left open in 1979 about their “other solutions” — where an independent integer programme shows the optimal distributions number exactly three, and the decision shows exactly one of them is realisable (the other two are not, upgrading MPR’s tentative single-case report to a proof covering both). Full attribution is given, with primary-source quotations and explicit translation conventions.

Independently of the odd-square results, we classify the 19 86619\,866 previously released 304304-edge C4C_{4}-free subgraphs of Q7Q_{7} (exactly 389389 of them odd-square) into 2020 dimension-profile types, establish their common structural core (degree sequence {432,596}\{4^{32},5^{96}\}, spectral radius in [4.78543,4.79129][4.78543,4.79129], local maximality — properties of the released catalogue, not claims about all 304304-edge solutions), and decompose them into 180180 Aut⁡(Q7)\mathrm{Aut}(Q_{7})-orbits containing 34 227 20034\,227\,200 labelled solutions, of which the released files are 0.058%0.058\%; whether these are all orbits of 304304-edge solutions is open. This revision adds an orbit-witness certificate whose standard-library checker verifies the orbit assignment in seconds (hence “at most 180180 orbits”); its --canonical mode certifies “exactly 180180” independently of the full group-action scan that produced the decomposition. For Q6Q_{6}, the unrestricted value ex⁡(Q6,C4)=132\mathrm{ex}(Q_{6},C_{4})=132 rests on Harborth–Nienborg’s combinatorial upper bound, which we did not independently verify; the odd-square g⁡(6)=132g(6)=132 is self-contained here. Every certified or deterministic numerical claim — those backed by a released certificate or by a bundled deterministic computation — is re-checkable from the released code and data; one-off historical observations and the one imported exact result (the unrestricted n=6n=6 upper bound) are marked as such throughout, and the released repository is accompanied by SHA-256 manifests. Edge lists and code:
https://github.com/minamominamoto/c4free-hypercube.

This is a revision of a manuscript first circulated as arXiv:2603.29127 (v1–v4, March–May 2026); v1 appeared as “New Lower Bounds for C4C_{4}-Free Subgraphs of the Hypercubes Q7Q_{7} and Q8Q_{8}”, and by v4 the title had become “New Lower Bounds for C4C_{4}-Free Subgraphs of the Hypercubes Q6Q_{6}, Q7Q_{7}, and Q8Q_{8}: Constructions, Structure, and Computational Method.” That earlier version announced ex⁡(Q8,C4)≥680\mathrm{ex}(Q_{8},C_{4})\geq 680 and did not include the odd-square material of Section 6; see the Acknowledgements for the circumstances of the revision. Three further claims of v1–v4 are withdrawn or corrected here, and are recorded as such rather than quietly dropped. (i) Its Section 7 was titled “Computational Proof that ex⁡(Q6,C4)=132\mathrm{ex}(Q_{6},C_{4})=132” and asserted that standard MIP solvers verify the instance quickly; we were unable to close the optimality gap (Section 9), so that section is retitled and the upper bound ex⁡(Q6,C4)≤132\mathrm{ex}(Q_{6},C_{4})\leq 132 again rests solely on Harborth–Nienborg [11]. (ii) Its abstract gave the pairwise Hamming range of the Q7Q_{7} catalogue as 3636–260260; that came from a 5 0005\,000-pair sample, disclosed only in the body. Exhaustive computation over all 197 319 045197\,319\,045 pairs gives 66–274274 (Section 7.3), so both endpoints were substantially wrong and the inference that the solutions lie far apart does not survive. (iii) Its degree sequence for the 132132-edge Q6Q_{6} construction, {432,532}\{4^{32},5^{32}\}, is arithmetically impossible — the degree sum is 288288, i.e. 144144 edges — and the correct sequence is {456,58}\{4^{56},5^{8}\} (Section 8.5); the “degree support {n−3,n−2,n−1}\{n-3,n-2,n-1\}” regularity suggested there rested on that error and is withdrawn. The extrapolated Brass–Harborth–Nienborg entries for n=4,5,6n=4,5,6 in v1–v4’s value table are likewise replaced by explicit out-of-domain markers (Table 1).

1 Introduction

The nn-dimensional hypercube QnQ_{n} has vertex set {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n}, two vertices adjacent iff they differ in exactly one coordinate; it has 2n2^{n} vertices and n⋅2n−1n\cdot 2^{n-1} edges. The problem of determining ex(Qn,C4)=max{|E(G)|:G⊆Qn,G is C4-free}\mathrm{ex}(Q_{n},C_{4})=\max\{|E(G)|:G\subseteq Q_{n},\,G\text{ is }C_{4}\text{-free}\} was raised by Erdős [9] and remains open in general.

The best known asymptotic bounds are

12​(n+n)⋅2n−1≤ex⁡(Qn,C4)(n=4r),ex⁡(Qn,C4)≤(0.60318+o⁡(1))⋅n⋅2n−1,\tfrac{1}{2}(n+\sqrt{n})\cdot 2^{n-1}\;\leq\;\mathrm{ex}(Q_{n},C_{4})\quad(n=4^{r}),\qquad\mathrm{ex}(Q_{n},C_{4})\;\leq\;(0.60318+o(1))\cdot n\cdot 2^{n-1}, (1)

where the lower bound is due to Brass, Harborth, and Nienborg [3] and holds, in this form, only when nn is a power of 44; the side condition is attached to the displayed inequality rather than left to the surrounding text, since the two halves of (1) have different scopes. The upper bound is a statement about the edge Turán density πe=lim supnex⁡(Qn,C4)/(n​2n−1)\pi_{e}=\limsup_{n}\mathrm{ex}(Q_{n},C_{4})/(n2^{n-1}), not a pointwise inequality valid at every finite nn; the constant 0.603180.60318 is due to Baber [1], who used the semidefinite flag algebra method to improve the earlier bound of Thomason and Wagner [16]; the intermediate value 0.60680.6068 is due to Balogh, Hu, Lidický, and Liu [2]. For general n≥9n\geq 9, the weaker bound 12​(n+0.9​n)⋅2n−1\tfrac{1}{2}(n+0.9\sqrt{n})\cdot 2^{n-1} applies [3]. A wording caution is useful for cross-checking the literature: LNSW26’s discussion of this BHN expression contains a sentence calling it an “at most” bound (the sentence persists in the published version’s Introduction, which we checked directly), whereas BHN95’s own statement gives both expressions as lower bounds on the maximum edge count, which settles the direction at the source. We flag this explicitly as a direction slip in that secondary description rather than an alternative theorem: an “at most” reading is internally untenable at n=16n=16: BHN’s tight n=4rn=4^{r} form is a lower bound, ex⁡(Q16,C4)≥(16+4)⋅214=327 680\mathrm{ex}(Q_{16},C_{4})\geq(16+4)\cdot 2^{14}=327\,680, while the alleged reading would assert the upper bound ex⁡(Q16,C4)≤(16+0.9⋅4)⋅214=321 126.4\mathrm{ex}(Q_{16},C_{4})\leq(16+0.9\cdot 4)\cdot 2^{14}=321\,126.4 — a certified lower bound exceeding the alleged upper bound, a contradiction. We follow BHN95. Exact values have been determined for small nn; Harborth and Nienborg [11] proved ex⁡(Q6,C4)=132\mathrm{ex}(Q_{6},C_{4})=132.

Our main theorem determines the extremal value g⁡(n)g(n) within the odd-square subclass — edge sets meeting every square in an odd number of edges — exactly for n=6,7,8n=6,7,8, in certificate form; as the attribution immediately below and Section 6 spell out, the new content is the machine-verifiable certificates and the short self-contained proof, not the bound values themselves:

Theorem 1 (Exact odd-square values).

g⁡(6)=132g(6)=132, g⁡(7)=304g(7)=304, and g⁡(8)=682g(8)=682. The numerical values for n=6,7n=6,7 have historical priority in Derrida–Pomeau–Toulouse–Vannimenus [5], and MPR95 [15] reported attainment of the corresponding n=8n=8 ground-state bound. The assertion here is a self-contained graph-theoretic re-proof/certification of those values, not a claim that the three numbers themselves are new.

The attribution of the three values, kept in one place (the detailed record with primary-source quotations is Section 6; everywhere else defers here):

nn value g⁡(n)g(n): priority contribution here
66 attained by DPTV79 (D=6D{=}6 ground state); value attributed to LNSW26 by [13] certificate; short proof
77 DPTV79 (explicit D=7D{=}7 construction) certificates; short proof
88 MPR95 (attainment reported in energy units, no data) 682682-edge translation; certificate; short proof

Here “short proof” means Lemma 12’s self-contained derivation of the optima DPTV tabulate; in no row are the numerical values themselves claimed as new. One caveat travels with the n=6n=6 row: DPTV79’s Table I could not be text-extracted from the scans we obtained, so the identification of its “other solutions” with our distributions A and B rests on the completeness of our own enumeration together with the surrounding prose, not on a direct transcription (disclosed in Section 6); the exhaustive realisability decision itself is independent of that reading.

All three values are self-contained within the released materials: each upper bound follows from Lemma 9 and Lemma 12 (Section 6.2), and each lower bound is witnessed by an explicit, machine-verified odd-square edge list released with this paper (Section 6.3). The citations to [5, 15] record historical priority for the values, not a dependency of the proofs. One point of possible confusion: the released 132-edge Q6Q_{6} construction q6_edges_132.jsonl is a genuine, independently machine-verified C4C_{4}-free witness for ex⁡(Q6,C4)≥132\mathrm{ex}(Q_{6},C_{4})\geq 132, but it is not odd-square; the odd-square witness for g⁡(6)≥132g(6)\geq 132 is the separate file q6_odd_square_132.json.

Corollary 2 (Certified lower bounds).

ex⁡(Q7,C4)≥304\mathrm{ex}(Q_{7},C_{4})\geq 304 and ex⁡(Q8,C4)≥682\mathrm{ex}(Q_{8},C_{4})\geq 682.

Both parts follow immediately from Theorem 1 (proved in Section 6) via g⁡(n)≤ex⁡(Qn,C4)g(n)\leq\mathrm{ex}(Q_{n},C_{4}), redundantly with the explicit constructions of Sections 4–5. Neither bound value is new, and the history is stated plainly here, once. The Q7Q_{7} value follows from DPTV79’s explicit 1979 construction [5]; we present it as an independently reproduced, machine-verified result. For Q8Q_{8} (improving our originally announced 680680), MPR95 [15] report — in a single unelaborated sentence, with no spin configuration and no machine-checkable artefact — a D=8D=8 ground state attaining Derrida et al.’s improved bound. They state the value as −361-361 on the D=9D{=}9 comparison scale they use across dimensions: a normalised per-spin energy times their factor 768768, not a count of couplings or any other absolute integer of the D=8D{=}8 model (Section 6 gives the conversion; in their text the attainment statement and the integer occur in two separate sentences, combined here). Via the signed-graph/odd-square correspondence this would imply a 682682-edge odd-square subgraph of Q8Q_{8}, but as an uncertificated existence claim we do not treat it as settling the question on its own. What we add at n=8n=8 is the explicit edge-count translation (Section 6.2); two released 682682-edge certificates — the regenerable q8_A_witness.json, re-derivable end-to-end from seed 9000890008 (Section 6.3), and the historical first witness q8_odd_square_682.json, whose dated private-correspondence provenance is disclosed there — and the structural analysis of Proposition 15. The other supplementary constructions are q7_edges_304.jsonl.part1--3 for Q7Q_{7} and the originally announced 680-edge q8_edges_680.jsonl, retained as a simulated-annealing data point (Section 5).

What the corollary does not resolve is whether these bounds are exact, i.e. whether ex⁡(Q7,C4)=304\mathrm{ex}(Q_{7},C_{4})=304 and ex⁡(Q8,C4)=682\mathrm{ex}(Q_{8},C_{4})=682: a general C4C_{4}-free subgraph need not be odd-square, so g⁡(n)=ex⁡(Qn,C4)g(n)=\mathrm{ex}(Q_{n},C_{4}) does not follow automatically, and of the 19 86619\,866 published 304-edge Q7Q_{7} solutions, only 389 are odd-square (Section 7).

Four caveats attach to Table 1. First, Eq. (1)’s tight form applies only for n=4rn=4^{r} and its weaker form only for n≥9n\geq 9 [3], so the n=5,6n=5,6 entries are not covered by either stated form (marked n/a) and the n=7,8n=7,8 entries lie beyond the stated domain of both forms (marked †\dagger): the out-of-domain extrapolations of the n≥9n\geq 9 form evaluate there to ≈300.2\approx 300.2 and ≈674.9\approx 674.9 respectively, figures recorded here only, for illustrative comparison, never as proven bounds; no claim in this paper depends on them. Second, the n=4n=4 value admits a two-line proof, recorded here because we could not locate an explicit page-level statement of it in the literature (not in [4], and neither OEIS A245762 nor the Emléktábla collection attributes the n=4n=4 entry individually): Q4Q_{4} has (42)⋅22=24\binom{4}{2}\cdot 2^{2}=24 squares and each edge lies in exactly n−1=3n-1=3 of them, so a C4C_{4}-free subgraph must omit at least one edge of every square and hence omit at least ⌈24/3⌉=8\lceil 24/3\rceil=8 of the 3232 edges, giving ex⁡(Q4,C4)≤24\mathrm{ex}(Q_{4},C_{4})\leq 24; the matching construction is the n=4rn=4^{r} case (r=1r=1) of Brass–Harborth–Nienborg [3], whose lower bound 12​(n+n)​2n−1\tfrac{1}{2}(n+\sqrt{n})2^{n-1} evaluates to exactly 2424 there. Third, in the Source column, “value; witness ours” means the numerical value has historical priority in the cited work, which published no machine-readable edge list or spin configuration for it; the explicit certificate released here is the present author’s own and is not claimed to reproduce any configuration of the cited work. Fourth (‡\ddagger), the n=6n=6 upper bound ex⁡(Q6,C4)≤132\mathrm{ex}(Q_{6},C_{4})\leq 132 is used here on the authority of [11] and has not been independently re-verified in this work (our own ILP attempt did not close the optimality gap, Section 9.2); the odd-square value g⁡(6)=132g(6)=132 is self-contained and unaffected.

The paper is organised as follows. Section 2 collects scope, attribution, the verification map, and the provenance record in one place (material that earlier revisions carried in the abstract). Section 3 describes the C4C_{4} enumeration and verification procedure used throughout. Sections 4–5 present the originally announced Q7Q_{7} and Q8Q_{8} simulated-annealing constructions. Section 6 introduces the odd-square subclass, proves Theorem 1, and presents the reconstructed 682-edge Q8Q_{8} witness and its verification. Section 7 classifies the 19 86619\,866 Q7Q_{7} solutions found by their dimension profiles, yielding exactly 20 types, and reports the odd-square audit (389 of 19 866). Section 8 describes the two-phase simulated annealing algorithm. Section 9 reproduces ex⁡(Q6,C4)=132\mathrm{ex}(Q_{6},C_{4})=132 computationally on the lower-bound side, with an ILP formulation for the upper-bound side. Section 10 lists open problems.

2 Reader’s Guide: Scope, Attribution, and Provenance

This section collects in one place the scope limitations, the attribution record with primary-source detail, the map of what is certified and how to check it, and the provenance of the released constructions. Earlier revisions carried this material in the abstract; the abstract now summarises, and this section is the authoritative expanded statement. Nothing here is new relative to the previous revision except where explicitly marked; the text is relocated, not retracted. One reading convention, stated once here instead of piecemeal: several quantities reported in this paper (for example the square split in Proposition 13(ii), the Tr⁡(A4)\operatorname{Tr}(A^{4}) value in Proposition 19(iii), and the h≥0h\geq 0 restriction of Lemma 11) are arithmetically forced by the edge count, the degree sequence, or the odd-square condition rather than independent findings; where this happens the text marks them as consistency checks, and they should be read as such, not as separate results. A second convention of the same kind: every certified mathematical claim in this paper depends only on artefacts bundled with the release; the items individually marked as reported-but-not-auditable (S. Lai’s independent cross-check, the recovered 7272-hour solver log, the SAT/MIP trial statistics, and MPR95’s energy inputs) support the provenance and attribution narrative only, never a theorem.

After this manuscript was first circulated, a reader (S. Lai) identified an overlooked connection to a line of statistical-physics literature on fully frustrated hypercubes: under the standard correspondence between edge sets meeting every 44-cycle (square) an odd number of times and fully frustrated signed hypercubes, the 1979 construction of Derrida, Pomeau, Toulouse, and Vannimenus [5] already yields a D≤7D\leq 7 odd-square construction attaining 304304 edges at D=7D=7 (we did not reconstruct their specific H7H_{7} edge set), and the D=8D{=}8 ground state reported by Marinari, Parisi, and Ritort [15] yields a 682-edge C4C_{4}-free subgraph of Q8Q_{8} that improves our originally announced 680-edge construction. For Q7Q_{7}, this value (304304) is also attained by 389389 of our own previously found 304-edge solutions, which we confirm independently satisfy the odd-square condition (none is claimed to be DPTV’s specific H7H_{7} construction; we only confirm the attained value, not edge-set identity with theirs). For Q8Q_{8}, we derived and machine-verified an explicit 682-edge witness whose local-field sum S=340S=340 converts under MPR95’s Hamiltonian H/N=−S/(288)H/N=-S/(2^{8}\sqrt{8}) to their reported improved D=8D=8 bound on the common comparison scale (Section 6.2); we use the same canonical fully frustrated coupling that MPR95 write explicitly (their Eq. 4; derivation documented in Section 6.3); this witness is not claimed to be a reconstruction of any particular configuration MPR may have used internally, since they did not publish one. This 682-edge witness is presented here as the paper’s headline lower bound in place of the earlier 680-edge witness.

Writing g⁡(n)g(n) for the maximum size of an odd-square edge set (every square meets it in exactly one or three edges), the numerical values g⁡(6)=132g(6)=132, g⁡(7)=304g(7)=304, and g⁡(8)=682g(8)=682 are, in physics terms, already implicit in the literature: Derrida, Pomeau, Toulouse, and Vannimenus [5] explicitly construct fully-frustrated ground states for d≤7d\leq 7 (giving g⁡(6)g(6) and g⁡(7)g(7) under the correspondence below), and Marinari, Parisi, and Ritort [15] report having obtained, by simulated annealing, a D=8D=8 ground state attaining Derrida et al.’s improved energy lower bound (giving g⁡(8)g(8) under the same correspondence). Neither the field identity nor its use to bound g⁡(n)g(n) is new: Derrida, Pomeau, Toulouse, and Vannimenus [5] derive the same identity in 1979 by the same argument (a sum over sites in which the frustration of every plaquette cancels the cross terms), note explicitly that it survives restriction to one side of the bipartition, pose exactly the integer optimisation problem Section 6.2 solves, and tabulate its optimum for n≤10n\leq 10 (their Table I). What Table I lists is the energy bound EdE_{d} together with the counts n⁡(h)n(h) (its caption describes a ground-state-energy lower bound with the corresponding internal-field distributions; on their scale Ed=−h¯E_{d}=-\bar{h}, a sign-only relabelling of the mean field, so we write what the table actually prints); the corresponding value S=72S=72 at n=6n=6 is our conversion, not a figure they state, just as the SS values we read off MPR95’s energies are ours rather than theirs. In their notation the n=6n=6 optimum is realised by what they call the “first solution” (n⁡(4)=6,n⁡(2)=24,n⁡(0)=2)(n(4){=}6;\,n(2){=}24;\,n(0){=}2), matching our own independently recomputed optimum exactly. The graph-theoretic formulation connecting the fully-frustrated signed hypercube to the C4C_{4}-free extremal problem is likewise anticipated by Laplante, Naserasr, Sunny, and Wang [14], who study the frustration index of the fully-frustrated signature directly in these terms (as a graph-theoretic problem they describe, to the best of their knowledge, as previously untreated) (Section 6.2 below). Given this, our contribution at n=6,7,8n=6,7,8 is narrower than a first reading of Theorem 1 might suggest, and consists of three parts, none of which is the numerical values 72,160,34072,160,340 themselves: (i) a short self-contained proof (Lemma 12, a mod-88 refinement of the classical two-point inequality) of the optima DPTV tabulate. DPTV formulate the same constrained optimisation over integer distributions, imposing the same parity and sign conditions, and give its best values and the attaining distributions in their Table I; what Lemma 12 adds is a derivation short enough to check by hand, from which those values — and the number of distributions attaining them — follow without the table. It is an alternative route to their results, not a correction or a strengthening of them; (ii) explicit, machine-verifiable edge-list certificates realising the bound at all three of n=6,7,8n=6,7,8 – DPTV’s own realisations are figures and prose for n≤7n\leq 7 only, n=8n=8 being left open by them and later claimed, without any released data, by Marinari, Parisi, and Ritort [15]; we are not aware of an earlier publicly released explicit odd-square edge list with a dedicated verifier for the n=8n=8 case, nor of an earlier such certificate for the n=6n=6 case. This is deliberately a limited priority statement rather than a claim of exhaustive bibliographic priority: we have not surveyed every literature and data release since 1979; for n=6n=6, for instance, OEIS A245762 lists a⁡(6)=132a(6)=132 with an extensions credit to M. Scheucher and P. Tabatabai (2015) for supplying the term, while citing Harborth–Nienborg [11] for the result itself; it links generator scripts, though not an odd-square edge list. Note also that the values g⁡(n)g(n) for n≤6n\leq 6, including g⁡(6)=132g(6)=132, are attributed to LNSW26 by [13], so at n=6n=6 what is offered here is a certificate for a known value, not the value; and (iii) an exhaustive decision, in Section 6.3, of a question DPTV posed and left open in 1979 – which of the several n=6n=6 optima described in their Table I are actually realisable by a spin configuration. MPR95 had already addressed this question by simulated annealing, reporting that only the first is realisable and that “the other” seems not to be; we reduce it to a finite (2322^{32}) search, decide it in seconds, and thereby upgrade that tentative report to a proof covering both non-realisable distributions. Here the prior literature’s constructions are not machine-readable in the same sense: DPTV79 give an explicit recursive scaling construction (their bond configurations for H5,H6,H7H_{5},H_{6},H_{7}, described in prose and figures, not released as a computer-readable edge list), while MPR95 report in a single sentence that they exhibited a D=8D=8 ground state matching the improved energy bound, with a method description (simulated annealing) and the bound value (−361-361 on the D=9D{=}9 comparison scale they use for bound values across dimensions, not an absolute integer of the D=8D{=}8 model; see Section 6), but no machine-checkable certificate: no spin configuration, no edge list, and no graph-theoretic translation – an existence claim we can neither independently verify nor extend beyond matching its numerical value. The same holds at n=6n=6, where DPTV79’s own D=6D=6 configuration is described in prose; we construct an independent 132-edge odd-square edge list instead, which happens to realise the local-field distribution they report as their table’s first solution. Beyond matching that one, Section 6.3 reports a targeted computational search for the other two optimal n=6n=6 distributions DPTV79’s Table I lists but do not know to be realisable; extensive simulated annealing (q6_other_distributions.py) never reaches either, plateauing at the same nonzero distance from target across every one of 40 and 20 deterministically specified RNG seeds respectively (the consecutive integer seed lists are protocol labels, not a claim of statistically independent random draws), while the same search method reaches the realised distribution in every trial. This is computational evidence, not a proof; Proposition 14 now supplies one (Section 6.3). The exact value ex⁡(Q6,C4)=132\mathrm{ex}(Q_{6},C_{4})=132 of Harborth and Nienborg [11] is therefore no longer needed to bound g⁡(6)g(6) from above, though it remains the source for the unrestricted value. This settles the odd-square subclass completely for n=6,7,8n=6,7,8 without resolving the unrestricted problem ex⁡(Qn,C4)\mathrm{ex}(Q_{n},C_{4}), since a general C4C_{4}-free subgraph need not be odd-square.

An exhaustive audit of the 19 86619\,866 previously published 304304-edge Q7Q_{7} solutions shows that only 389389 of them lie in the odd-square subclass; the remaining 19 47719\,477 do not. The odd-square construction therefore does not subsume or fully explain the structural classification given here (one profile type, Type 18 with 101 solutions, is entirely odd-square; of the other 19, three (ranks 5, 7, and 10) are mixed, containing some odd-square and some non-odd-square solutions, and the remaining 16 contain no odd-square solutions at all): the 19 86619\,866 solutions’ common structural core (degree sequence {432,596}\{4^{32},5^{96}\}, spectral radius in [4.78543,4.79129][4.78543,4.79129], local maximality) and their classification into 20 dimension-profile types are independent results. These 19 86619\,866 labelled solutions certainly do not exhaust all labelled 304-edge C4C_{4}-free subgraphs of Q7Q_{7}: the first released solution alone has a stabiliser of size 33 in Aut⁡(Q7)≅(ℤ2)7⋊S7\mathrm{Aut}(Q_{7})\cong(\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{7}\rtimes S_{7} (order 645 120645\,120; exhaustive check over all 645 120645\,120 elements), consisting of the identity and two nontrivial elements, both coordinate permutation ++ XOR pairs. We write a permutation as the tuple pp with the meaning “bit ii of vv becomes bit p⁡[i]p[i] of the image”, the convention of type18_automorphisms.py. (In symbols this is the scatter form imp⁡[i]=vi\mathrm{im}_{p[i]}=v_{i}, equivalently the gather form imj=vp−1​[j]\mathrm{im}_{j}=v_{p^{-1}[j]}; the census and witness scripts implement exactly this map, so a reader re-deriving the masks below should read the tuple this way and not as “image bit ii equals vv’s bit p⁡[i]p[i]”.) Under v↦π⁡(v⊕m)v\mapsto\pi(v\oplus m) (XOR first, then permute) the two elements are then (5,1,2,3,4,6,0)(5,1,2,3,4,6,0) with mask m=33=01000012m=33=0100001_{2} and its square (6,1,2,3,4,0,5)(6,1,2,3,4,0,5) with m=96=11000002m=96=1100000_{2}; under v↦π⁡(v)⊕mv\mapsto\pi(v)\oplus m the two masks are interchanged. The group itself, and the fact that its order is 33, are of course independent of both conventions; only the labelling of the masks is not. They together form a cyclic group of order 33 – so its orbit alone has size 645 120/3=215 040>19 866645\,120/3=215\,040>19\,866. Decomposing the whole catalogue (Proposition 20) makes this quantitative: the 19 86619\,866 fall into 180180 orbits whose lengths sum to 34 227 20034\,227\,200, so the released files are 0.058%0.058\% of the labelled solutions in those orbits alone. What remains open is whether they represent every Aut⁡(Q7)\mathrm{Aut}(Q_{7})-orbit of 304-edge C4C_{4}-free subgraphs, not whether they exhaust the labelled solutions themselves; see Open Problem 3.

For Q8Q_{8}, the reconstructed 682-edge odd-square witness is locally maximal in a strong sense: all 342 non-edges of Q8Q_{8} create at least 3 new C4C_{4}s upon addition (compared with the earlier 680-edge simulated-annealing Solution B, for which 2 of 344 non-edges created only 1 or 2 new C4C_{4}s; see Section 5 for both 680-edge solutions released). Every C4C_{4}-free-construction bound reported here, and every one of the three odd-square values, is witnessed by an explicit edge-list construction with a machine-verifiable certificate. Two distinct 132132-edge Q6Q_{6} constructions are released and should not be conflated: q6_edges_132.jsonl is C4C_{4}-free but not odd-square (its square-intersection histogram is {1:8, 2:44, 3:188}\{1{:}8,\,2{:}44,\,3{:}188\}) and establishes ex⁡(Q6,C4)≥132\mathrm{ex}(Q_{6},C_{4})\geq 132, while q6_odd_square_132.json is the odd-square witness for g⁡(6)≥132g(6)\geq 132 (histogram {1:30, 3:210}\{1{:}30,\,3{:}210\}). For every bound, a complete, deterministic enumeration of all four-cycles (240 for Q6Q_{6}, 672 for Q7Q_{7}, 1 792 for Q8Q_{8}) establishes C4C_{4}-freeness, and every construction certificate reported here (the edge sets themselves, their C4C_{4}-freeness, and the Q6Q_{6} and Q8Q_{8} odd-square conditions) is reproducible by a dependency-free verifier that is independent of all search and generation code (verify.py; implementation-level independence is supplied separately by the bundled second implementation cross_verify.py described in Section 2), with the Q7Q_{7} odd-square membership of individual solutions separately reproducible via audit_q7_odd_square.py. The further structural and statistical claims reported below (spectral-radius ranges, pairwise Hamming extrema, Type-18 automorphism counts, non-edge violation distributions, and similar) are largely recomputable from the released code: analyze_q7_structure.py reproduces the degree sequence, the 20 direction profiles, the spectral-radius range, and the exhaustive pairwise Hamming statistics (minimum 66, maximum 274274, mean 195.396108​…195.396108\ldots, median 196196), and type18_automorphisms.py reproduces the Type-18 automorphism counts; reproduce_core.py drives the certificate and decision checks in one command, and reproduce_core.py --structural additionally runs the Q7Q_{7} structural and Hamming analyses (which need numpy and several minutes). The count of 636636 minimum-distance pairs and their breakdown into 2828 profile-type combinations are produced by q7_hamming_tally.py, which recovers all pairwise distances from a single blocked matrix product (using |E​△​E′|=2​(304−|E∩E′|)|E\triangle E^{\prime}|=2(304-|E\cap E^{\prime}|)) in a few seconds and optionally writes the minimum-distance pairs to CSV.

The Q7Q_{7} solutions were found by a two-stage process that we have since traced and partly re-verified (the two stages have different evidentiary status, detailed below and in Section 8): a conventional multi-move-type penalty simulated annealing (add/remove/11-swap/kick moves with temperature-scaled Boltzmann acceptance) found a single seed 304304-edge solution, and a remove-and-repair collector – starting from an existing solution (optionally transformed by a random element of Aut⁡(Q7)\mathrm{Aut}(Q_{7})), removing a few edges, then greedily re-adding only violation-free edges – mass-collected the released 19 86619\,866 solutions; we directly confirmed the collector stage by running it ourselves: from the released seed, in one unseeded 3030-second run we observed 1 9871\,987 new valid solutions. The script sets no random seed, so this exact count is an observed throughput datum rather than a bit-for-bit reproducibility target; separate reruns have shown the same qualitative rapid collection without being used as additional numerical evidence here. Tracing further back, we located most of the prior history, with one correction to an earlier draft of this paper: the earliest recovered attempt (a CBC-solver ILP explicitly commented as attacking Erdős’s $100 problem) has a confirmed bug (its C4C_{4}-detection finds 00 of 672672 four-cycles, since adjacent vertices in the bipartite Q7Q_{7} never share a common neighbour, which its logic incorrectly relies on), so we withdraw our earlier claim that this specific recovered file is what reached 289289 edges; a recovered solver log, headed as a corrected version and reporting the correct C4C_{4} count, documents that a since-fixed version of the script did reach 289289 edges, but we have not located that corrected script itself. From there, file timestamps together with recovered solver logs and a chat transcript document a progression 289→293→299→301→303→304289\to 293\to 299\to 301\to 303\to 304 edges, the last step apparently via the sa_search.py series. We confirmed the 301301-edge step’s mechanism directly: source.py, the HiGHS version, run for 6060 seconds with no prior solution to warm-start from (a genuine cold start), produces a valid, growing 295295-edge C4C_{4}-free solution via branch-and-bound alone. We further ran a format/implementation-consistency check that any reader can reproduce from the released files alone, without needing our recovered archive: applying sa_collect304.py’s own canonicalisation-then-MD5 hash function directly to each of the 19 86619\,866 released edge sets reproduces the hash field already stored in that same released record, for all 19 86619\,866 (Section 8); this shows the released hash field and script are mutually consistent, not that this script historically produced these edge sets, which remains a separate, historical-record claim (recovered logs, chat transcript, timestamps). The two released Q8Q_{8} 680680-edge solutions (Solutions A and B, Section 5) have likewise now been traced to recovered, independently-verified working code, sa_q8.py: a penalty-SA hill-climber that always restarts each trial from the current best valid (zero-violation) solution rather than from a fresh random sample, progressively improving it (initial greedy construction →\to intermediate saved states at 584,662,…,679584,662,\ldots,679 edges →\to 680680). We confirmed the two files this recovered code produced – named q8_edges_680.txt and q8_best.json in the recovered archive, released here as q8_solution_a.txt and q8_solution_b.json – match Solutions A and B respectively exactly by edge set, and we confirmed the code makes genuine progress on direct execution: run once under an external 9090-second timeout from a saved 670670-edge intermediate state, it reduced the violation count at the 675675-edge target from 2222 to 88. sa_q8.py sets no random seed, so this specific numeric trajectory is a one-time observation, not a fixed-seed reproducible result: a reader rerunning the released files should expect qualitatively similar monotonic improvement, not these exact numbers. Separate unseeded reruns from the same checkpoint also showed qualitative improvement, but their concrete counts are omitted here because no corresponding logs or fixed seeds are released. This is a different script, released separately from c4free_sa.py, whose generalisation of the same two-phase idea to a single nn-agnostic script (Section 8) does not share this always-restart-from-a-valid-state property, and which we found cannot progress from a fresh random start under its own documented parameters for either Q7Q_{7} or Q8Q_{8}; c4free_sa.py is retained as released (with its defect documented) but is no longer the operative account of how either the Q7Q_{7} or the Q8Q_{8} solutions were produced. For Q6Q_{6} we additionally give an ILP formulation whose feasible value matches the known exact value ex⁡(Q6,C4)=132\mathrm{ex}(Q_{6},C_{4})=132; we did not independently verify the ILP’s optimality within a practical runtime. The upper bound itself rests on the combinatorial proof of Harborth and Nienborg [11]; independently, we reproduce the matching lower-bound construction.

Edge lists, ILP files, the odd-square reconstruction and audit scripts, and source code are made available at
https://github.com/minamominamoto/c4free-hypercube . The repository is synchronised with each released revision; readers should check the commit corresponding to this version, since files introduced by a revision appear only from that commit onward – here, among others: q6_decide_realizability.py, solve_field_ip.py, and the Q8Q_{8} second-distribution witnesses. The authoritative file list for this revision, with SHA-256 sums, is given by the three manifests in the accompanying archive: ORIGINAL_DATA_SHA256SUMS.txt, ODDSQUARE_BRIDGE_SHA256SUMS.txt, and MANUSCRIPT_SHA256SUMS.txt; the last covers this document’s own .tex and .pdf so that a reader can confirm which revision a given file set belongs to.

3 C4C_{4} Enumeration and Verification

Lemma 3 (C4C_{4} enumeration in QnQ_{n}).

Every four-cycle of QnQ_{n} is uniquely determined by a pair of coordinate directions 0≤i<j≤n−10\leq i<j\leq n-1 and a base vertex b∈{0,1}nb\in\{0,1\}^{n} with bi=bj=0b_{i}=b_{j}=0. Its four vertices are

b,b⊕ei,b⊕ej,b⊕ei⊕ej,b,\quad b\oplus e_{i},\quad b\oplus e_{j},\quad b\oplus e_{i}\oplus e_{j},

and the total number of four-cycles in QnQ_{n} is (n2)⋅2n−2\binom{n}{2}\cdot 2^{n-2}: there are (n2)\binom{n}{2} choices of the two varying coordinates and, after forcing those two base bits to 00, exactly 2n−22^{n-2} choices for the remaining base bits. For n=6n=6: 240240; for n=7n=7: 672672; for n=8n=8: 1 7921\,792.

Verification algorithm. Given a candidate edge set E⊆E⁡(Qn)E\subseteq E(Q_{n}) stored as a hash set (of unordered pairs {u,v}\{u,v\}, so u​vuv and v​uvu are the same element), the following procedure performs a complete, deterministic C4C_{4}-freeness check:

for each pair (i,j)(i,j) with 0≤i<j≤n−10\leq i<j\leq n-1:
 for each b∈{0,1}nb\in\{0,1\}^{n} with bi=bj=0b_{i}=b_{j}=0:
  let v1=b,v2=b⊕ei,v3=b⊕ej,v4=b⊕ei⊕ejv_{1}=b,\;v_{2}=b\oplus e_{i},\;v_{3}=b\oplus e_{j},\;v_{4}=b\oplus e_{i}\oplus e_{j}
  if {v1​v2,v1​v3,v2​v4,v3​v4}⊆E\{v_{1}v_{2},\,v_{1}v_{3},\,v_{2}v_{4},\,v_{3}v_{4}\}\subseteq E: return violation
return c4-free

We applied this algorithm to all constructions and all 19 86619\,866 solutions of Q7Q_{7}; every call returned c4-free.

4 The Q7Q_{7} Construction

We constructed a C4C_{4}-free subgraph of Q7Q_{7} on 304 edges by penalty-based simulated annealing (Section 8, where the production code has since been recovered and verified), then certified it by Lemma 3’s algorithm. This construction is released as selected_edges_best.json, and its edge set is identical to global index 00 of the 19 86619\,866-solution catalogue (first line of q7_edges_304.jsonl.part1) – so every property below is directly checkable from either file.

Proposition 4.

The specific 304304-edge seed construction just described (the first solution found, not a generic member of the later 19 86619\,866-solution ensemble of Section 7) has the following properties:

  1. (i)

    Degree sequence: 32 vertices of degree 4 and 96 of degree 5 (degree sum 608=2⋅304608=2\cdot 304).

  2. (ii)

    Spectral radius λ1≈4.787\lambda_{1}\approx 4.787 (a genuine computed quantity for this construction); λmin≈−4.787\lambda_{\min}\approx-4.787, i.e. λ1+λmin=0\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{\min}=0 to machine precision, which is automatic for any subgraph of the bipartite Q7Q_{7} and serves here only as a sanity check on the eigenvalue computation, not as an independent structural finding.

  3. (iii)

    Tr⁡(A4)=5216\mathrm{Tr}(A^{4})=5216, attaining the C4C_{4}-free trace equality ∑ideg⁡(i)2+∑u​v∈E(deg⁡u+deg⁡v)−2​|E|\sum_{i}\deg(i)^{2}+\sum_{uv\in E}(\deg u+\deg v)-2|E|. Like the item above this is forced by the degree sequence rather than independent of it: the two summands are equal because ∑u​v∈E(deg⁡u+deg⁡v)=∑vdeg⁡(v)2\sum_{uv\in E}(\deg u+\deg v)=\sum_{v}\deg(v)^{2} (each vertex’s degree is counted once per incident edge), so the expression is 2​∑vdeg⁡(v)2−2​|E|2\sum_{v}\deg(v)^{2}-2|E|; the equality of Tr⁡(A4)\mathrm{Tr}(A^{4}) with it is where C4C_{4}-freeness enters — every off-diagonal entry of A2A^{2} is then 00 or 11, so ∑i≠j(A2)i​j2=∑i≠j(A2)i​j=∑vdeg⁡(v)​(deg⁡(v)−1)\sum_{i\neq j}(A^{2})_{ij}^{2}=\sum_{i\neq j}(A^{2})_{ij}=\sum_{v}\deg(v)(\deg(v)-1). See Proposition 19(iii).

  4. (iv)

    Local maximality: every non-edge of Q7Q_{7} creates a C4C_{4} when added.

Across the collector runs described in Section 8 (whose trial field reaches into the millions per run; 19 86619\,866 is the number of stored solutions, not the number of trials), we obtained 19 86619\,866 C4C_{4}-free subgraphs of Q7Q_{7} on 304 edges with pairwise distinct edge sets (not quotiented by Aut⁡(Q7)\mathrm{Aut}(Q_{7}); this catalogue-level distinctness is asserted mechanically by verify.py, which hashes each sorted edge list and requires all 19 86619\,866 digests to differ – a separate check from its per-solution duplicate-edge test), all sharing the structural properties stated in Proposition 19.

5 The Q8Q_{8} Construction

This section documents the originally announced Q8Q_{8} witness, found by a penalty-SA hill-climber distinct from the Q7Q_{7} construction’s method (see Section 8 for the recovered and verified sa_q8.py production code). It has since been superseded as the paper’s headline lower bound by the 682-edge odd-square reconstruction of Section 6; it is retained here as an independent structural data point.

Simulated annealing produced the two C4C_{4}-free subgraphs of Q8Q_{8} on 680 edges (both released in q8_edges_680.jsonl), each certified by exhaustive enumeration of all 1 7921\,792 four-cycles. We refer to them as Solution A (first line of the file) and Solution B (second line); the two are structurally distinct and are kept separate below, since an earlier draft of this section inadvertently described properties of Solution A and Solution B as if they belonged to a single construction.

Proposition 5.

Both 680-edge solutions are C4C_{4}-free and locally maximal (every non-edge of Q8Q_{8} creates at least one C4C_{4} upon addition – that is, maximal with respect to edge addition; throughout this paper “locally maximal” means exactly this and implies no stronger optimality notion), with edge density 680/1024=66.4%680/1024=66.4\% (compared with 304/448=67.9%304/448=67.9\% for the Q7Q_{7} construction) and λ1+λmin=0\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{\min}=0 (automatic for any subgraph of the bipartite Q8Q_{8}; not by itself a distinguishing structural feature). They differ as follows:

  1. (i)

    Solution A: degree sequence {48, 5160, 688}\{4^{8},\,5^{160},\,6^{88}\} (degree sum 1360=2⋅6801360=2\cdot 680); square-intersection histogram {:308,:1484}\{1\!:\!308,\,3\!:\!1484\} over the 1 7921\,792 squares (incidentally odd-square, though not constructed as such – see below for the implication of this); non-edge violation distribution {:3,:48,:144,:136,:13}\{2\!:\!3,\,3\!:\!48,\,4\!:\!144,\,5\!:\!136,\,6\!:\!13\} (minimum 22 new C4C_{4}s per non-edge).

  2. (ii)

    Solution B: degree sequence {47, 5162, 687}\{4^{7},\,5^{162},\,6^{87}\} (degree sum 1360=2⋅6801360=2\cdot 680); square-intersection histogram {:302,:12,:1478}\{1\!:\!302,\,2\!:\!12,\,3\!:\!1478\} (not odd-square: 1212 squares meet it in exactly 22 edges); non-edge violation distribution {:1,:1,:49,:153,:124,:16}\{1\!:\!1,\,2\!:\!1,\,3\!:\!49,\,4\!:\!153,\,5\!:\!124,\,6\!:\!16\} (minimum 11 new C4C_{4}, attained by exactly one non-edge).

Solution A’s odd-squareness has a notable implication for the timeline of results in this paper: since it was originally announced (before the 682682-edge odd-square reconstruction of Section 6 existed) and is itself odd-square, the bound g⁡(8)≥680g(8)\geq 680 was already achieved within the odd-square subclass at that earlier point, not only via the later, deliberately-constructed 682682-edge witness. We did not notice or exploit this at the time; it is recorded here as a fact about the released data, confirmed independently by direct square-by-square enumeration.

Remark 6.

Brass–Harborth–Nienborg’s tight bound 12​(n+n)⋅2n−1\tfrac{1}{2}(n+\sqrt{n})\cdot 2^{n-1} applies only for n=4rn=4^{r}, and their weaker bound 12​(n+0.9​n)⋅2n−1\tfrac{1}{2}(n+0.9\sqrt{n})\cdot 2^{n-1} is stated only for n≥9n\geq 9 (Eq. (1), [3]); neither covers n=8n=8. Evaluating the n≥9n\geq 9 form at n=8n=8 nonetheless gives ≈674.9\approx 674.9; both 680-edge constructions and the 682-edge odd-square reconstruction of Section 6 exceed this extrapolated figure (by 5.1 and 7.1 edges respectively), but we do not claim this as a comparison against a proven bound.

5.1 Local optimality of the 680-edge constructions

Solution B is locally maximal in the weakest possible sense among the two: among its 344344 non-edges, exactly 11 creates exactly 11 new C4C_{4}; exactly 11 creates exactly 22; the remaining 342342 create 33 or more (Proposition 5(ii)). Solution A’s non-edges all create at least 22 new C4C_{4}s.

For historical completeness only, not as a reviewable computational result: the manuscript that originally announced the 680680-edge construction also reported a failed search for 681681 edges. No seed list or run log survives for that negative-search statistic, and the originally associated conjecture ex⁡(Q8,C4)=680\mathrm{ex}(Q_{8},C_{4})=680 is false in view of the 682-edge witness. We therefore omit the old numerical trial count from the evidentiary record and retain only the fact that an unarchived failed search was reported, which we mention only as development history, not as evidence bearing on any current claim in this paper.

Table 2 compares the Q7Q_{7} construction with Solution B (the 680-edge solution whose local-optimality numbers are discussed above); see Table 3 in Section 6 for the odd-square reconstructions.

6 The Odd-Square Subclass

6.1 Definition and equivalence to fully frustrated hypercubes

Definition 7.

An edge set E⊆E⁡(Qn)E\subseteq E(Q_{n}) is odd-square if every square (four-cycle) of QnQ_{n} meets EE in an odd number of edges, i.e. one or three of its four edges lie in EE. Write g⁡(n)=max⁡{|E|:E​ is odd-square in ​Qn}g(n)=\max\{|E|:E\text{ is odd-square in }Q_{n}\}.

Every odd-square edge set is C4C_{4}-free, since no square can meet it in all four edges; hence g⁡(n)≤ex⁡(Qn,C4)g(n)\leq\mathrm{ex}(Q_{n},C_{4}). The odd-square condition is exactly the condition studied under a different name in the statistical-physics literature on fully frustrated hypercubes: assign to each edge ee a sign σ⁡(e)=+1\sigma(e)=+1 if e∈Ee\in E and σ⁡(e)=−1\sigma(e)=-1 otherwise; the square condition becomes “the product of signs around every square is −1-1”, i.e. every square is frustrated.

Lemma 8.

Let σ1,σ2:E⁡(Qn)→{±1}\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}:E(Q_{n})\to\{\pm 1\} both have product −1-1 on every square. Then there is a function t:{0,1}n→{±1}t:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\} with σ2​(x,y)=σ1​(x,y)​t​(x)​t​(y)\sigma_{2}(x,y)=\sigma_{1}(x,y)\,t(x)t(y) for every edge (x,y)(x,y).

Proof.

Let τ=σ1​σ2\tau=\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2} (pointwise product). On every square CC,

∏e∈Cτ⁡(e)=(∏e∈Cσ1​(e))​(∏e∈Cσ2​(e))=(−1)​(−1)=+1.\prod_{e\in C}\tau(e)=\Bigl(\prod_{e\in C}\sigma_{1}(e)\Bigr)\Bigl(\prod_{e\in C}\sigma_{2}(e)\Bigr)=(-1)(-1)=+1.

The map sending a cycle CC to ∏e∈Cτ⁡(e)∈{±1}\prod_{e\in C}\tau(e)\in\{\pm 1\} is a group homomorphism from the cycle space of QnQ_{n} (over GF⁡(2)\mathrm{GF}(2), under symmetric difference) to {±1}\{\pm 1\}: an edge lying in both cycles disappears from their symmetric difference and contributes τ​(e)2=+1\tau(e)^{2}=+1 to the product of their images, so additive cancellation in GF⁡(2)\mathrm{GF}(2) matches multiplicative cancellation in {±1}\{\pm 1\} — which is exactly the homomorphism property. The squares of QnQ_{n} generate its cycle space (a standard fact for hypercubes: every cycle is a symmetric difference of squares – for general nn this follows, e.g., from the theorem that every partial cube has a cycle basis consisting of convex cycles [7], the convex cycles of QnQ_{n} being exactly its squares; the bundled deterministic script cycle_space_rank.py verifies this by direct GF⁡(2)\mathrm{GF}(2) rank computation for every nn used in this paper, asserting that the rank of the square incidence vectors equals the cycle-space dimension E−V+1=(n−2)​2n−1+1E-V+1=(n-2)2^{n-1}+1 for each of n=3,…,8n=3,\ldots,8 – the six dimensions being 55, 1717, 4949, 129129, 321321 and 769769), so this homomorphism is determined by its values on the squares; since it is +1+1 on every square, it is +1+1 on every cycle. A signature with product +1+1 on every cycle of a connected graph is a coboundary: τ⁡(x,y)=t⁡(x)​t​(y)\tau(x,y)=t(x)t(y) for some t:V→{±1}t:V\to\{\pm 1\} (the classical balance theorem for signed graphs, Harary [8]). Solving for σ2\sigma_{2} gives the claim. ∎

Lemma 8 says any two odd-square signatures are related by a vertex switching tt. For a fixed coupling JJ, letting the spin configuration s:V⁡(Qn)→{±1}s:V(Q_{n})\to\{\pm 1\} range over all 22n2^{2^{n}} choices (a sign at each of the |V⁡(Qn)|=2n|V(Q_{n})|=2^{n} vertices, hence 2|V|=22n2^{|V|}=2^{2^{n}} assignments) produces exactly the signatures σs​(x,y)=J⁡(x,y)​s​(x)​s​(y)\sigma_{s}(x,y)=J(x,y)s(x)s(y) in the switching class of JJ (writing s=t⋅s0s=t\cdot s_{0} for a fixed reference s0s_{0} realises every switching tt); this is the operational fact we use, not a claim that different ss give the same energy under fixed JJ (they generally do not – that variation is exactly what is being optimised). The energy-preserving gauge transformation in the physical sense instead acts on both JJ and ss together, J⁡(x,y)↦J⁡(x,y)​t​(x)​t​(y)J(x,y)\mapsto J(x,y)t(x)t(y) and s⁡(x)↦t⁡(x)​s​(x)s(x)\mapsto t(x)s(x), under which J⁡(x,y)​s​(x)​s​(y)J(x,y)s(x)s(y) is unchanged edge-by-edge [15]. Consequently, g⁡(n)g(n) — defined as a maximum over all odd-square edge sets — equals the maximum of |E||E| over the switching class of any one fixed fully-frustrated signature, in particular the reference coupling JJ used in Section 6.3’s witness; optimising that one fixed JJ (or, for D=8D=8, exhibiting a ground state attaining Derrida et al.’s improved energy lower bound for it, as Marinari–Parisi–Ritort report [15]) therefore does optimise over the class defining g⁡(n)g(n), not merely over a possibly-proper subclass of it. (The inclusion that makes this an equality of classes is Lemma 8 read in the other direction: the fixed JJ’s negative edge set is itself odd-square, so by the lemma every odd-square edge set is switching-equivalent to it, and hence lies in that single switching class.)

Under the further correspondence between signed hypercubes and Ising spin configurations s:{0,1}n→{±1}s:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{\pm 1\} via σ⁡(x,y)=J⁡(x,y)​s​(x)​s​(y)\sigma(x,y)=J(x,y)\,s(x)s(y) for a fixed reference coupling JJ with every square frustrated, maximising |E||E| (i.e. maximising the number of positive edges, equivalently minimising the number of negative edges) is exactly the problem of minimising the ground-state energy of the fully frustrated Ising hypercube studied by Derrida, Pomeau, Toulouse, and Vannimenus [5] and, for D=8D=8, by Marinari, Parisi, and Ritort [15]: the ground-state energy is (up to an affine rescaling) the number of negative edges, |E⁡(Qn)|−|E||E(Q_{n})|-|E|. In the language of signed graphs, |E⁡(Qn)|−g⁡(n)|E(Q_{n})|-g(n) is the frustration index of the fully frustrated signature on QnQ_{n}. Laplante, Naserasr, Sunny, and Wang [14] study this frustration index directly (in the context of Huang’s proof of the sensitivity conjecture, and as a target they describe as not previously treated in the literature to the best of their knowledge) and explicitly establish a connection between it and Erdős’s question on the largest C4C_{4}-free subgraph of the hypercube, giving lower and upper bounds on the frustration index of the fully frustrated signature that match when nn is a power of 44; our g⁡(6),g⁡(7),g⁡(8)g(6),g(7),g(8) results above sharpen this connection to exact values at n=6,7,8n=6,7,8 specifically. To quantify that sharpening: our exact frustration indices are 60,144,34260,144,342 at n=6,7,8n=6,7,8 (i.e. |E⁡(Qn)|−g⁡(n)|E(Q_{n})|-g(n)). A baseline lower bound LNSW26 state as Theorem 5.2 (which they attribute to an implication of Bialostocki’s work [10]) — and which is, in our notation, exactly the Cauchy–Schwarz relaxation S≤Q​m=n​ 2n−1S\leq\sqrt{Q\,m}=\sqrt{n}\,2^{n-1} of Lemma 9, already recorded by DPTV79 (p. 620) as giving “a first lower bound for the ground state energy” — F⁡(Hn,σ∗)≥(n−n)⋅2n−2F(H_{n},\sigma^{*})\geq(n-\sqrt{n})\cdot 2^{n-2}, which evaluates to ≥57,≥140,≥331\geq 57,\geq 140,\geq 331 at n=6,7,8n=6,7,8 respectively – looser than our exact values by 3,4,113,4,11. LNSW26’s own contribution beyond this baseline is a matching upper bound on the frustration index (equivalently, a lower bound on g⁡(n)g(n)) via a construction that coincides with Brass–Harborth–Nienborg’s [3] when nn is a power of 44; for n=6,7,8n=6,7,8 (not powers of 44) this upper bound is strictly looser than the lower bound, so LNSW26’s bounds do not determine g⁡(n)g(n) at these values. The sharpening therefore applies at n=7,8n=7,8 but not at n=6n=6: the 20th Emléktábla Workshop problem collection [13] credits LNSW26 with the exact values g⁡(n)=1,3,9,24,56,132g(n)=1,3,9,24,56,132 for n≤6n\leq 6. (During source verification we obtained and read the LNSW26 preprint in full, and, on 26 August 2026, the published version’s full text (ACM Trans. Comput. Theory 18(1), Art. 6); the value list appears in neither, so this attribution rests on [13] alone; nor do LNSW26’s own published theorems determine g⁡(6)g(6), since their upper and lower bounds close only at powers of 44.) The attribution is therefore secondary-source only: if it is right (say via a version or communication we have not seen), the record of g⁡(6)=132g(6)=132 predates us in LNSW26; in any case we do not claim the value as new here, and its historical attainment is DPTV79’s: their D=6D=6 ground state has 6060 negative bonds out of 192192 (p. 622), i.e. 132132 positive edges, and MPR95 note that constructions saturating the improved bound exist for D≤7D\leq 7. What Lemma 12 adds at n=6n=6 is a short self-contained derivation of a known value; at n=7,8n=7,8 it tightens the frustration-index lower bound by 44 and 1111, and the explicit witnesses of Section 6.3 close the gap from the construction side, giving exact values where the general bounds leave a nonzero interval. This sign convention matches the one used by the reconstruction script generate_q8_682.py (Section 6.3), where EE is exactly the set of edges with J⁡(x,dim)​s​(x)​s​(y)=+1J(x,\mathrm{dim})\,s(x)s(y)=+1; for a vertex vv of degree degE⁡(v)\deg_{E}(v) in EE, we call h⁡(v)=2​degE⁡(v)−nh(v)=2\deg_{E}(v)-n its local field under this convention (matching the local-field histogram reported in Proposition 15 below). We do not reproduce Derrida et al.’s derivation of the local-field lower bound here, and do not need to: Section 6.2 derives the bounds it uses from Lemmas 9 and 12 directly, and cites [5, 15] only for historical priority. Their results are stated there for reference — established for D≤7D\leq 7 by explicit construction, and used by Marinari–Parisi–Ritort at D=8D=8 — and the corresponding witnesses are constructed and verified independently in Section 6.3. One asymmetry of rigour is acknowledged explicitly: we have not machine-verified that DPTV79’s own H6,H7H_{6},H_{7} bond configurations satisfy the odd-square condition at the certificate level at which our own edge lists are verified. For their constructions the property follows from the correspondence (Lemma 8: the positive-edge set of any spin configuration under a fully frustrated coupling is odd-square) applied to their stated construction, not from a data-level check, which is impossible because no machine-readable configuration of theirs was ever published.

This connection was brought to our attention, after the original circulation of this manuscript, by S. Lai (see Acknowledgements), who identified the relevance of [5, 15] and located the improved Q8Q_{8} result.

6.2 Exact values for n=6,7,8n=6,7,8

Derrida et al. [5] give a local-field lower bound on the number of negative (frustrated, in their terminology) edges, tight enough to determine the fully frustrated hypercube’s ground-state energy exactly for D≤7D\leq 7 via an explicit recursive construction, and conjectured it remains tight for D≥8D\geq 8. For D=6D=6, they give this explicit construction directly: “this configuration for H6H_{6} contains 60 negative bonds (out of a total of 192)” [5, p. 622], i.e. 192−60=132192-60=132 positive (unfrustrated) edges, with the construction guaranteed fully frustrated (every square meeting it in an odd number of negative edges) by their general recursive method. Under the correspondence of Section 6 this is an explicit odd-square witness with 132132 edges, so g⁡(6)≥132g(6)\geq 132. We cite this for historical priority only: the lower bound g⁡(6)≥132g(6)\geq 132 is established below by an explicit odd-square edge list of our own (Section 6.3, q6_odd_square_132.json), and the matching upper bound g⁡(6)≤132g(6)\leq 132 follows from Lemma 9 and Lemma 12 without appeal to [11]. We did not reconstruct DPTV’s specific D=6D=6 bond configuration, though their recursion determines the edge counts without it.11 1 What follows is arithmetic within DPTV’s construction, recorded for the reader’s convenience; no claim in this paper depends on it. DPTV’s construction builds HdH_{d} from Hd−3H_{d-3} by replacing each vertex with a supersite. Counting negative bonds through the recursion gives 12+6+6=2412+6+6=24 at d=5d=5: four H3H_{3} supersites contribute 4×3=124\times 3=12 internal negative bonds, the three white superbonds contribute 3×2=63\times 2=6, and the one black superbond contributes 1×6=61\times 6=6. At d=6d=6, eight H3H_{3} supersites contribute 8×3=248\times 3=24; the minimal H3H_{3} pattern has three black and nine white superbonds, contributing 3×6=183\times 6=18 and 9×2=189\times 2=18, for 6060 total — exactly the figure DPTV state in the text. At d=7d=7, the minimal H4H_{4} pattern has 1616 supersites and 3232 superbonds, eight black and twenty-four white, giving 16×3+8×6+24×2=14416\times 3+8\times 6+24\times 2=144, i.e. 448−144=304448-144=304 positive edges. So the value 304304 follows from their construction by a few lines of arithmetic, even though we do not exhibit their H7H_{7} edge set. At d=8d=8 the pattern is H5H_{5} (3232 vertices, 8080 bonds, minimal negative count 2424, matching r⁡(5)=56r(5)=56 positive): 3232 supersites and 8080 superbonds, 2424 black and 5656 white, give 32×3+24×6+56×2=35232\times 3+24\times 6+56\times 2=352 negative bonds, i.e. r⁡(8)=1024−352=672r(8)=1024-352=672 — the Open Problem 8 table entry whose gap of 1010 to the field bound 682682 is discussed there. our witness is an independent one, which however turns out to realise the same local-field distribution they report (see Section 6.3).

Lemma 9 (Field identity, after Derrida–Pomeau–Toulouse–Vannimenus).

For any odd-square edge set EE in QnQ_{n}, writing U={v∈{0,1}n:v​ has an even number of ​1​-bits}U=\{v\in\{0,1\}^{n}:v\text{ has an even number of }1\text{-bits}\} for the even-parity part of the bipartition of QnQ_{n} (|U|=2n−1|U|=2^{n-1}; the argument below is symmetric in UU and its complement, so this choice is only for concreteness and all numerical values reported for UU throughout this paper, e.g. Proposition 15’s hh-distribution, use this same convention) and h⁡(v)=2​degE⁡(v)−nh(v)=2\deg_{E}(v)-n as before, every h⁡(v)h(v) with v∈Uv\in U is an integer of the same parity as nn, and

∑v∈Uh​(v)2=n⋅2n−1.\sum_{v\in U}h(v)^{2}=n\cdot 2^{n-1}.
Proof.

For v∈Uv\in U and direction i∈{0,…,n−1}i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\} write si​(v)=σ⁡(v,v⊕ei)∈{±1}s_{i}(v)=\sigma(v,v\oplus e_{i})\in\{\pm 1\}, so h⁡(v)=∑isi​(v)h(v)=\sum_{i}s_{i}(v) — in particular h⁡(v)≡n(mod2)h(v)\equiv n\pmod{2}, being a sum of nn terms ±1\pm 1 (equivalently h⁡(v)=2​degE⁡(v)−nh(v)=2\deg_{E}(v)-n), which establishes the parity claim in the statement — and h​(v)2=n+∑i≠jsi​(v)​sj​(v)h(v)^{2}=n+\sum_{i\neq j}s_{i}(v)s_{j}(v). Fix i≠ji\neq j and consider, for v∈Uv\in U, the square on {v,v⊕ei,v⊕ej,z}\{v,v\oplus e_{i},v\oplus e_{j},z\} where z=v⊕ei⊕ej∈Uz=v\oplus e_{i}\oplus e_{j}\in U. Its four edges have signs si​(v)s_{i}(v), sj​(v)s_{j}(v), and (computed from zz’s own perspective, since a sign is a single scalar attached to the edge) sj​(z)s_{j}(z), si​(z)s_{i}(z). The odd-square condition means their product is −1-1 — recall the convention fixed at the start of this section: σ⁡(e)=+1\sigma(e)=+1 iff e∈Ee\in E, so a square meeting EE in an odd number of edges carries an odd number (44 minus an odd number, i.e. 11 or 33) of −1-1 factors among its four signs, and its sign product is −1-1; “odd-square” and “negative square” are the same condition under this convention. Thus: si​(v)​sj​(v)⋅sj​(z)​si​(z)=−1s_{i}(v)s_{j}(v)\cdot s_{j}(z)s_{i}(z)=-1. Writing X=si​(v)​sj​(v)X=s_{i}(v)s_{j}(v) and Y=si​(z)​sj​(z)Y=s_{i}(z)s_{j}(z), both lie in {±1}\{\pm 1\} and X​Y=−1XY=-1 forces X=−YX=-Y, i.e. si​(v)​sj​(v)+si​(z)​sj​(z)=0s_{i}(v)s_{j}(v)+s_{i}(z)s_{j}(z)=0. The map v↦z=v⊕ei⊕ejv\mapsto z=v\oplus e_{i}\oplus e_{j} is a fixed-point-free involution on UU (as ei⊕ej≠0e_{i}\oplus e_{j}\neq 0), so it partitions UU into pairs {v,z}\{v,z\} on each of which the two corresponding terms cancel; summing over all such pairs gives ∑v∈Usi​(v)​sj​(v)=0\sum_{v\in U}s_{i}(v)s_{j}(v)=0 for every fixed i≠ji\neq j. Summing over all ordered pairs i≠ji\neq j and adding the n⋅|U|n\cdot|U| diagonal contribution gives ∑v∈Uh​(v)2=n⋅2n−1\sum_{v\in U}h(v)^{2}=n\cdot 2^{n-1}. ∎

A scope note before the remark: the odd-square hypothesis enters this proof only square by square, through each individual sign product. The identity itself is exactly equivalent to the average form of that condition — by the remark below, a side UU satisfies ∑v∈Uh​(v)2=n⋅2n−1\sum_{v\in U}h(v)^{2}=n\cdot 2^{n-1} if and only if ∑ssplU⁡(s)=(n2)​ 2n−2\sum_{s}\operatorname{spl}_{U}(s)=\binom{n}{2}\,2^{n-2} — and this average route is how the 19 47719\,477 non-odd-square catalogue solutions satisfy it as well, forced by their shared degree sequence (Proposition 19(i)).

Remark 10 (Exact defect formula).

The bookkeeping in this proof runs without the odd-square hypothesis and yields an exact formula for arbitrary edge sets. For any E⊆E⁡(Qn)E\subseteq E(Q_{n}), call a square ss UU-split at its even-parity corner vv if exactly one of the two edges of ss incident to vv lies in EE (equivalently si​(v)​sj​(v)=−1s_{i}(v)s_{j}(v)=-1 for the direction pair {i,j}\{i,j\} of ss), and let splU⁡(s)∈{0,1,2}\operatorname{spl}_{U}(s)\in\{0,1,2\} count the even-parity corners of ss at which it is UU-split. Each square has exactly two even-parity corners, related by v↦v⊕ei⊕ejv\mapsto v\oplus e_{i}\oplus e_{j} (a map that changes exactly two bits and so preserves parity), and belongs to exactly one direction pair; running the ordered-pair sum of the proof without the cancellation step, each square contributes 2−2​splU​(s)2-2\operatorname{spl}_{U}(s) once per ordering of its direction pair, so

∑v∈Uh​(v)2=n⋅2n−1+n⁡(n−1)​ 2n−1−4​∑ssplU⁡(s)=n2​ 2n−1−4​∑ssplU⁡(s),\sum_{v\in U}h(v)^{2}=n\cdot 2^{n-1}+n(n-1)\,2^{n-1}-4\sum_{s}\operatorname{spl}_{U}(s)=n^{2}\,2^{n-1}-4\sum_{s}\operatorname{spl}_{U}(s),

the sum running over all (n2)​ 2n−2\binom{n}{2}\,2^{n-2} squares of QnQ_{n}. Hence the identity ∑v∈Uh​(v)2=n⋅2n−1\sum_{v\in U}h(v)^{2}=n\cdot 2^{n-1} holds for a given side of the bipartition if and only if ∑ssplU⁡(s)=(n2)​ 2n−2\sum_{s}\operatorname{spl}_{U}(s)=\binom{n}{2}\,2^{n-2}, i.e. iff squares are UU-split at exactly one even-parity corner on average. The odd-square condition forces the pointwise version: a sign product −1-1 over the four edges of ss means si​(v)​sj​(v)=−si​(z)​sj​(z)s_{i}(v)s_{j}(v)=-s_{i}(z)s_{j}(z) at its two even-parity corners, so splU⁡(s)=1\operatorname{spl}_{U}(s)=1 for every ss, and symmetrically on the odd-parity side. We use the average-split reformulation diagnostically, not as a search filter: evaluating ∑ssplU⁡(s)\sum_{s}\operatorname{spl}_{U}(s) already inspects every square, so it is no cheaper than the odd-square test itself. The bundled deterministic script field_identity_defect.py verifies the formula – and every numerical instance of it quoted in this paper – on the released certificates and on random edge sets, using only the standard library.

This proof uses only that every square has product −1-1 (the odd-square condition), so it is sufficient for the identity to hold; it is not necessary. Testing against all 19 86619\,866 published 304304-edge Q7Q_{7} solutions – odd-square and non-odd-square alike – shows every one of them satisfies ∑v∈Uh​(v)2=448\sum_{v\in U}h(v)^{2}=448, including the 19 47719\,477 that are not odd-square. This is explained, for these particular solutions, by a simpler fact that does not need odd-squareness either: every one of the 19 86619\,866 has all degrees in {4,5}\{4,5\} (Proposition 19), and since Q7Q_{7} is bipartite, ∑v∈Udeg⁡(v)=|E|=304\sum_{v\in U}\deg(v)=|E|=304 exactly (every edge has exactly one endpoint in UU); writing a,ba,b for the number of degree-44, degree-55 vertices in UU (a+b=64a+b=64), 4​a+5​b=3044a+5b=304 forces b=48,a=16b=48,a=16 regardless of which specific 304304-edge solution is chosen, so h⁡(v)=2​deg⁡(v)−7∈{1,3}h(v)=2\deg(v)-7\in\{1,3\} takes value 11 on exactly 1616 vertices of UU and 33 on the other 4848, giving ∑v∈Uh​(v)2=16⋅12+48⋅32=16+432=448\sum_{v\in U}h(v)^{2}=16\cdot 1^{2}+48\cdot 3^{2}=16+432=448 automatically. We verified the UU-side split is indeed exactly {416,548}\{4^{16},5^{48}\} for all 19 86619\,866, with no exceptions. The identity’s failure for the non-odd-square Q8Q_{8} Solution B of Section 5 (1016≠10241016\neq 1024 on UU, while the complementary side gives exactly 10241024 — so only one side breaks) is therefore not explained by odd-squareness as such: Solution B is locally maximal, like Solution A, but with the smallest possible margin: its non-edge violation multiset is {1:1,2:1,3:49,4:153,5:124,6:16}\{1{:}1,2{:}1,3{:}49,4{:}153,5{:}124,6{:}16\}, so every missing edge still creates at least one C4C_{4}, though one of them creates exactly one (against a minimum of 22 for Solution A). It has an asymmetric degree distribution between UU and its complement ({43,582,643}\{4^{3},5^{82},6^{43}\} vs. {44,580,644}\{4^{4},5^{80},6^{44}\}), whereas Solution A, all 19 86619\,866 Q7Q_{7} solutions, and the 682682-edge witness all have symmetric UU/complement degree distributions. This symmetry is not itself implied by odd-squareness, however: a small odd-square counterexample in Q3Q_{3} (vertices 0,…,70,\ldots,7, E={(0,2),(2,6),(3,7),(4,5),(4,6),(6,7)}E=\{(0,2),(2,6),(3,7),(4,5),(4,6),(6,7)\}, whose six squares meet EE, in the direction-pair-then-base enumeration order of Lemma 3, in 1,3,1,3,3,11,3,1,3,3,1 edges) has UU-degree multiset {1,1,1,3}\{1,1,1,3\} against {0,2,2,2}\{0,2,2,2\} on the complement, while still satisfying ∑v∈Uh​(v)2=∑v∈Uch​(v)2=12=3⋅22\sum_{v\in U}h(v)^{2}=\sum_{v\in U^{c}}h(v)^{2}=12=3\cdot 2^{2} on each side separately. Remark 10 settles the identity’s exact logical status for arbitrary edge sets: it holds on a side iff squares are split at one corner of that side on average, ∑ssplU⁡(s)=(n2)​ 2n−2\sum_{s}\operatorname{spl}_{U}(s)=\binom{n}{2}\,2^{n-2}. Odd-squareness is the pointwise case (splU⁡(s)=1\operatorname{spl}_{U}(s)=1 for every square, both sides at once), and the average can be met without it: the catalogue’s very first record – the non-odd-square solution mentioned in Section 6.2 – has per-square split histogram {0:60, 1:552, 2:60}\{0{:}60,\,1{:}552,\,2{:}60\} on UU, sixty deficits exactly cancelled by sixty excesses for a total of 672=(72)​ 25672=\binom{7}{2}\,2^{5}, against the pointwise {1:672}\{1{:}672\} of the odd-square record 3434. So the identity is neither a characterisation of odd-squareness (the Q3Q_{3} example just given is odd-square without the UU/complement symmetry that holds for all 19 86619\,866 Q7Q_{7} solutions, and record 00 satisfies the identity without being odd-square) nor a coincidence specific to the released catalogue (for the 19 86619\,866 it is a forced consequence, via Proposition 19 and ∑v∈Udeg⁡(v)=|E|\sum_{v\in U}\deg(v)=|E|, of any 304304-edge subgraph of Q7Q_{7} having all degrees in {4,5}\{4,5\} – a structural fact about that particular edge count, established independently of odd-squareness). The one-sided failure of the Q8Q_{8} Solution B noted above is likewise quantified exactly by the formula: on its failing side ∑ssplU⁡(s)=1794=1792+2\sum_{s}\operatorname{spl}_{U}(s)=1794=1792+2, accounting for ∑v∈Uh​(v)2=1024−4⋅2=1016\sum_{v\in U}h(v)^{2}=1024-4\cdot 2=1016, while the complementary side has exactly 17921792 splits and sum 10241024. field_identity_defect.py recomputes each of these numbers from the released certificates.

The next lemma sits on no critical path in this paper: no upper- or lower-bound argument below uses it (as re-stated after Lemma 12). We record it because DPTV79 state the restriction and because the released witnesses satisfy it — forcedly, via their degree sequences.

Lemma 11 (Nonnegativity at the maximum).

If EE is odd-square in QnQ_{n} with |E||E| maximum (i.e. |E|=g⁡(n)|E|=g(n)), then h⁡(v)≥0h(v)\geq 0 for every v∈{0,1}nv\in\{0,1\}^{n}.

Proof.

Suppose h⁡(v)<0h(v)<0 for some vv. Flipping the spin at vv (replacing s⁡(v)s(v) by −s⁡(v)-s(v), all other spins unchanged) flips σ⁡(v,w)\sigma(v,w) for every edge (v,w)(v,w) incident to vv and leaves every other edge’s sign unchanged. Every square containing vv has exactly two edges incident to vv (the square’s other two edges are not incident to vv and their signs are untouched); flipping both leaves their product, and hence the whole square’s sign product, unchanged, so odd-squareness is preserved everywhere. At vv itself, the positive-edge count changes from p=(n+h⁡(v))/2p=(n+h(v))/2 to q=(n−h⁡(v))/2q=(n-h(v))/2, a change of q−p=−h⁡(v)>0q-p=-h(v)>0; no edge other than the nn edges incident to vv changes sign, so |E||E| increases by exactly −h⁡(v)>0-h(v)>0. This contradicts maximality of |E||E|, so no such vv exists. ∎

This is a corollary of, not an alternative to, Lemma 8: the argument uses only that flipping one vertex’s spin preserves odd-squareness (immediate from the switching correspondence) and counts the resulting change in |E||E| directly. All 389389 released odd-square Q7Q_{7} solutions have 304304 edges, which is the maximum by the upper bound g⁡(7)≤304g(7)\leq 304 proved below in Section 6.2 (the audit locating these 389 solutions is Section 7.4), so the Lemma’s hypothesis applies to every one of them; we checked h⁡(v)≥0h(v)\geq 0 on all 389389 with no counterexample — though, like the square split of Proposition 13(ii) and the Tr⁡(A4)\mathrm{Tr}(A^{4}) identity of Proposition 19(iii), this is forced rather than independent: Proposition 19(i) already pins every degree to {4,5}\{4,5\}, hence h=2​deg−7∈{1,3}h=2\deg-7\in\{1,3\}.

Given Lemma 9 alone, |E|=(n⋅2n−1+∑v∈Uh⁡(v))/2|E|=(n\cdot 2^{n-1}+\sum_{v\in U}h(v))/2 is bounded above by the integer optimisation problem of maximising ∑v∈Uh⁡(v)\sum_{v\in U}h(v) subject to the fixed sum of squares ∑v∈Uh​(v)2=n⋅2n−1\sum_{v\in U}h(v)^{2}=n\cdot 2^{n-1} over the 2n−12^{n-1} integers h⁡(v)h(v) of fixed parity (necessarily |h⁡(v)|≤n|h(v)|\leq n, since h⁡(v)=2​deg⁡(v)−nh(v)=2\deg(v)-n with 0≤deg⁡(v)≤n0\leq\deg(v)\leq n; the bundled solve_field_ip.py imposes that range explicitly, and dropping it changes neither the optima nor the number of optimal distributions) (we use only that every realisable hh-vector satisfies these constraints, not the converse that every integer vector satisfying them is realisable as an odd-square signature; the bound obtained is therefore an upper bound on |E||E|, tight whenever a matching witness is exhibited). This is essentially the optimisation problem DPTV79 pose immediately after their own derivation of Lemma 9: maximise h¯\bar{h} (their notation for the mean field) subject to the same sum-of-squares constraint, with one difference: DPTV79 additionally impose h≥0h\geq 0 before carrying out the distribution optimisation (p. 620, on the stated grounds that a ground-state search cannot have negative field values), whereas we drop that restriction entirely. The restriction is in fact vacuous for every nn: replacing hh by |h||h| preserves both the parity condition and ∑h2\sum h^{2} while not decreasing ∑h\sum h, so no optimal vector has a negative entry, and the two problems have the same optimum and the same optimal distributions at every nn. We none the less state the programme without the sign constraint, since the bound is then visibly independent of any positivity assumption. Their solution method is to observe that the optimal distribution concentrates on the integers nearest n\sqrt{n} – unique when exactly two suffice, multiple solutions (their Table I) when three or four are needed, which they note happens at n=6n=6 and n=8n=8 (p. 621) – and to tabulate the resulting optima for n≤10n\leq 10 by this reasoning rather than by a general closed-form argument. No sign hypothesis enters our derivation: the constraints admit negative hh, and Lemma 11 is not used. Its role is the separate one of describing configurations that actually attain the maximum (matching what we verified computationally on all 389389 odd-square Q7Q_{7} witnesses above).

The following elementary observation turns DPTV79’s “concentrate near n\sqrt{n}” heuristic into a closed form that is transparently exact and complete, without appeal to their table. It is the only ingredient beyond the classical two-point convexity inequality they already use.

Lemma 12 (Quantised two-point inequality).

Let aa be an integer of the same parity as nn and put b=a+2b=a+2. Then for every integer hh of the same parity as nn,

(h−a)​(h−b)≥ 0and(h−a)​(h−b)≡0(mod8).(h-a)(h-b)\ \geq\ 0\qquad\text{and}\qquad(h-a)(h-b)\equiv 0\pmod{8}.

In particular (h−a)​(h−b)∈{0,8,24,48,…}(h-a)(h-b)\in\{0,8,24,48,\ldots\}, so it is either 00 (exactly when h∈{a,b}h\in\{a,b\}) or at least 88.

Proof.

h−ah-a is even, say h−a=2​uh-a=2u with u∈ℤu\in\mathbb{Z}; then h−b=2​u−2h-b=2u-2, so (h−a)​(h−b)=4​u​(u−1)(h-a)(h-b)=4u(u-1). Consecutive integers u,u−1u,u-1 have product ≥0\geq 0 and even — one of the two is even — say u⁡(u−1)=2​ku(u-1)=2k with k≥0k\geq 0, so 4​u​(u−1)=8​k4u(u-1)=8k, a nonnegative multiple of 88; its successive values, at u∈{0,1},{−1,2},{−2,3},…u\in\{0,1\},\{-1,2\},\{-2,3\},\ldots, are 0,8,24,48,…0,8,24,48,\ldots It vanishes exactly when u∈{0,1}u\in\{0,1\}, i.e. h∈{a,b}h\in\{a,b\}. ∎

Summing Lemma 12 over v∈Uv\in U and writing S=∑v∈Uh⁡(v)S=\sum_{v\in U}h(v), m=|U|=2n−1m=|U|=2^{n-1}, Q=∑v∈Uh​(v)2=n⋅2n−1Q=\sum_{v\in U}h(v)^{2}=n\cdot 2^{n-1} gives the single inequality used for all three values of nn:

Δ:=∑v∈U(h(v)−a)(h(v)−b)=Q−(a+b)S+abm≥ 0,Δ≡(mod8).\Delta\ :=\ \sum_{v\in U}(h(v)-a)(h(v)-b)\ =\ Q-(a+b)S+ab\,m\ \geq\ 0,\qquad\Delta\equiv 0\!\!\pmod{8}. (2)

Before specialising, one relaxation is worth recording. Cauchy–Schwarz gives S≤Q​m=n​ 2n−1S\leq\sqrt{Q\,m}=\sqrt{n}\,2^{n-1} and hence |E|≤2n−2​(n+n)|E|\leq 2^{n-2}(n+\sqrt{n}) — the same expression as the Brass–Harborth–Nienborg lower bound in (1). So at n=4rn=4^{r} the two meet and g⁡(n)=2n−2​(n+n)g(n)=2^{n-2}(n+\sqrt{n}) exactly. For the lower-bound half of this equality it is not enough that BHN’s construction attains that edge count: g⁡(n)g(n) requires an odd-square set of that size, and this is precisely what LNSW26 supply — they prove that the BHN construction induces a signature of QnQ_{n} in which every 44-cycle is negative (equivalently, that the construction is odd-square), a fact they note does not follow from BHN’s original work ([14], Section 5.2 and Theorem 5.4; cf. Section 6 above). With that identification the BHN construction is optimal within the odd-square subclass at those nn. This is the shortest explanation of why LNSW26’s bounds close precisely at powers of 44, and it locates what Lemma 12 adds: at n=6,7,8n=6,7,8 the relaxation is not tight. At n=7n=7 nonnegativity alone already gives the exact S≤160S\leq 160, and at n=8n=8 integrality plus the parity of SS (each h⁡(v)h(v) has the parity of nn by Lemma 9, so SS is even) gives the exact S≤340S\leq 340; the mod-88 refinement is what is essential at n=6n=6, where it excludes S=74S=74. The nonnegativity is the classical bound S≤(Q+a​b​m)/(a+b)S\leq(Q+ab\,m)/(a+b); the congruence removes whatever residual gap elementary integrality and the parity of SS leave between that real bound and the true integer optimum – among our three instances this extra strength is needed only at n=6n=6, as the specialisations below make explicit. No computational filter is invoked in this modular step: Lemma 12 proves term by term that every summand in Δ\Delta is a nonnegative multiple of 88, so their sum has the same property. We apply (2) with the pair (a,b)(a,b) of parity-correct integers straddling the root-mean-square field Q/m=n\sqrt{Q/m}=\sqrt{n}, namely (1,3)(1,3) for n=7n=7 (7≈2.65\sqrt{7}\approx 2.65) and (2,4)(2,4) for n=6,8n=6,8 (6≈2.45\sqrt{6}\approx 2.45, 8≈2.83\sqrt{8}\approx 2.83); this is the minimising choice, and no search is needed to see it: putting u=a+1u=a+1 and Q=n​mQ=nm, the bound becomes

Q+a​b​ma+b=m2​(u+n−1u),\frac{Q+ab\,m}{a+b}=\frac{m}{2}\Bigl(u+\frac{n-1}{u}\Bigr),

which is decreasing for 0<u<n−10<u<\sqrt{n-1} and increasing thereafter, so the optimum over real uu is at u=n−1u=\sqrt{n-1}; since the admissible uu of the correct parity are spaced two apart, it suffices to evaluate the two straddling n−1\sqrt{n-1} and take the smaller. This gives (2,4)(2,4) at n=6n=6 (u=3u=3 against 5≈2.24\sqrt{5}\approx 2.24; the alternative (0,2)(0,2) has u=1u=1 and yields 9696), (1,3)(1,3) at n=7n=7, and (2,4)(2,4) at n=8n=8. n=6n=6. Here m=32m=32, Q=192Q=192, (a,b)=(2,4)(a,b)=(2,4), so Δ=448−6​S\Delta=448-6S.
